lessonTitle: Detecting and Reporting Adverse Reactions: Causality, Spontaneous Reporting and Allergy Counselling

blocks.text: A drug is licensed after trials involving a few thousand people. Once it is on the market, millions take it, and a rare reaction that occurs in one in ten thousand finally appears, scattered across clinics in different towns. No single doctor sees more than one case. The only thing that connects them is a form that each doctor chooses to fill in.

blocks.markdown: Clinical trials are too small, too short and too selective to detect rare or delayed adverse reactions, so safety monitoring continues after marketing (**pharmacovigilance**). Two tasks matter to the clinician: deciding whether a drug really caused a suspected reaction (**causality assessment**), and reporting it to the national scheme (**spontaneous reporting**) so that patterns across many patients can be identified.

blocks.title: Causality assessment
blocks.text: Causality assessment estimates the likelihood that a drug caused a given event. Structured tools such as the WHO-UMC categories (certain, probable, possible, unlikely, conditional, unassessable) and the Naranjo algorithm (a scored questionnaire) make the judgement explicit and reproducible.

items: Temporal relationship: did the event start after the drug and within a plausible time?
Dechallenge: did the event improve when the drug was stopped (positive dechallenge)?
Rechallenge: did it recur when the drug was restarted (positive rechallenge)? This is rarely done deliberately because of risk.
Alternative causes: could the underlying disease, other drugs or infection explain it?
Biological plausibility and prior reports: is the reaction known for this drug or class?
Dose relationship and laboratory evidence (such as drug level, or eosinophilia in an allergic reaction).

blocks.caption: WHO-UMC causality categories (summarised).
rows: Plausible time relationship; cannot be explained by disease or other drugs; positive dechallenge; pharmacologically definitive; rechallenge satisfactory if necessary
Reasonable time relationship; unlikely to be due to disease or other drugs; clinically reasonable response to withdrawal; rechallenge not required
Reasonable time relationship; could also be explained by disease or other drugs; information on withdrawal may be lacking or unclear
Time relationship improbable; other drugs or disease provide plausible explanations
More data needed, or information inadequate or contradictory

blocks.title: Applying a basic causality assessment
blocks.prompt: A 44-year-old woman develops an itchy maculopapular rash 6 days after starting co-trimoxazole for a urinary tract infection. The rash fades within 3 days of stopping co-trimoxazole. She has no other new drugs, no recent viral illness and no previous rash. Assess causality.

steps.text: Temporal relationship: onset 6 days after the first dose is a plausible time for a delayed cutaneous drug reaction.
Dechallenge: the rash resolved after the drug was withdrawn, a positive dechallenge.
Alternative causes: no other new drugs, and no infection or disease to explain the rash. Rash is a recognised reaction to co-trimoxazole.
Classification: the features match WHO-UMC 'probable'. It cannot be 'certain' because rechallenge was not performed, which would be unnecessary and potentially unsafe.
Action: record the reaction in the notes, label the allergy or intolerance accurately, and submit a report.

blocks.answer: Probable adverse drug reaction (WHO-UMC), recorded and reported

blocks.markdown: **Spontaneous reporting systems.** In the United Kingdom, suspected adverse drug reactions are reported to the MHRA through the **Yellow Card Scheme**, and in the United States to the FDA through **MedWatch**. Healthcare professionals and patients can report. Reports are pooled nationally and internationally (WHO Uppsala Monitoring Centre), and analysts look for **signals**: a pattern of reports suggesting a previously unrecognised or under-appreciated reaction. Newly marketed drugs and some biological medicines carry a **black triangle** in the UK to encourage reporting of all suspected reactions, however minor. Serious reactions should be reported for all drugs.

blocks.caption: Proportional reporting ratio. a = reports of the reaction of interest with the drug of interest; b = reports of all other reactions with that drug; c = reports of the reaction with all other drugs; d = reports of all other reactions with all other drugs. A PRR of 2 or more, with enough cases, is commonly used as a trigger for further review.

blocks.title: Detecting a disproportionality signal
blocks.prompt: In a database, drug X has 40 reports of hepatitis and 1960 reports of other reactions. All other drugs together have 500 reports of hepatitis and 49,500 reports of other reactions. Calculate the PRR. (Illustrative numbers.)

steps.text: Proportion of hepatitis among drug X reports: a/(a+b) = 40 / 2000 = 0.02.
Proportion among all other drugs: c/(c+d) = 500 / 50,000 = 0.01.

Interpretation: hepatitis is reported twice as often with drug X as with other drugs, which warrants review. It is a signal, not proof of causation, because reporting is influenced by publicity, prescribing patterns and under-reporting.

blocks.answer: PRR = 2: a potential signal needing further investigation

blocks.title: What spontaneous reporting can and cannot do
blocks.text: It is good for detecting rare, serious and unexpected reactions early and costs little. It cannot give incidence, because the number of patients exposed (the denominator) is unknown and most reactions go unreported. Signals are then tested with epidemiological studies.

blocks.markdown: **Counselling after a suspected drug allergy.** The aim is to protect the patient from re-exposure without applying a false label. Steps: (1) treat the acute reaction and document precisely what happened (drug, dose, timing, symptoms, severity, treatment); (2) record the allergy or intolerance in the notes and prescription chart; (3) explain to the patient in plain language which drug and related drugs to avoid, for example the penicillin class; (4) advise carrying an allergy alert (card, bracelet) and telling every prescriber and pharmacist; (5) give written information and, after anaphylaxis, adrenaline auto-injector training where indicated; (6) refer for specialist allergy assessment, since many reported allergies, particularly to penicillin, are not confirmed on testing; (7) inform the GP and report the reaction.

blocks.title: Accurate labels matter
blocks.text: Over-labelling (recording a side effect as an allergy) can lead to the use of less effective or more toxic alternatives, and missing a true allergy can be fatal. Record the nature of the reaction, not just the word allergy.

points: Causality is judged from time course, dechallenge, rechallenge, alternative causes and plausibility, using tools such as the WHO-UMC categories or Naranjo scoring.
Spontaneous reporting (Yellow Card, MedWatch) detects rare or new signals by pooling reports and looking for disproportionality, but cannot give incidence.
Counselling after a suspected allergy involves clear documentation, avoidance advice, allergy alert, specialist referral and reporting.

questions.stem: Which feature is most important to establish first when assessing whether a drug caused a suspected reaction?

options.text: Whether the event began after the drug was started, within a plausible time
The cost of the drug
Whether the drug has a brand name
The age of the prescriber

questions.correctOptionText: Whether the event began after the drug was started, within a plausible time

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a plausible temporal relationship is the basic requirement for causality.

questions.explanation: A drug cannot cause an event that began before it was taken, and the interval must fit the known mechanism. Temporal relationship is therefore the first test in causality assessment.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man develops cough after starting an ACE inhibitor. The cough stops within two weeks of stopping the drug. What does this observation represent?

options.text: A positive dechallenge, which supports a causal relationship
A negative dechallenge, which excludes causality
A positive rechallenge
Evidence that the reaction is Type B

questions.correctOptionText: A positive dechallenge, which supports a causal relationship

distractorRationale.a: Correct: improvement after withdrawal supports the drug as the cause.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: a negative dechallenge is lack of improvement.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: rechallenge means restarting the drug.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: classification by type is separate from dechallenge.

questions.explanation: Resolution of an event when the suspected drug is withdrawn is a positive dechallenge and increases the likelihood that the drug was responsible. It does not on its own prove causation.

questions.stem: A suspected reaction has a reasonable time relationship, is unlikely to be explained by the disease or other drugs, and improved on withdrawal, but no rechallenge was done. Which WHO-UMC category applies?

options.text: Probable
Certain
Unlikely
Unassessable

distractorRationale.a: Correct: these features define probable; rechallenge is not required.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: certain requires a definitive pharmacological or phenomenological explanation and rechallenge if necessary.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: the time relationship is plausible.

questions.explanation: WHO-UMC 'probable' requires a reasonable time relationship, an event unlikely to be due to other causes and a clinically reasonable response to withdrawal. Rechallenge is not required for this category.

questions.stem: In a safety database, drug Y has 24 reports of a particular reaction and 976 reports of other reactions. All other drugs together have 300 reports of the same reaction and 29,700 reports of other reactions. Calculate the proportional reporting ratio (PRR). (Illustrative numbers.)
questions.explanation: For drug Y the proportion is 24 / 1000 = 0.024; for other drugs it is 300 / 30,000 = 0.01. PRR = 0.024 / 0.01 = 2.4, above the commonly used threshold of 2, so the combination merits review.

questions.stem: A regional scheme receives 18 spontaneous reports of a reaction to a drug for which 120,000 prescriptions were dispensed in the same period. Calculate the crude reporting rate per 100,000 prescriptions.
questions.explanation: Reporting rate = 18 / 120,000 x 100,000 = 15 per 100,000 prescriptions. This is a crude indicator only, because under-reporting means the true incidence is higher and unknown.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes a limitation of spontaneous reporting schemes such as the Yellow Card scheme?

options.text: Under-reporting and lack of a denominator mean incidence cannot be calculated
They cannot detect rare reactions
They require rechallenge for every report
They only accept reports from pharmaceutical companies

questions.correctOptionText: Under-reporting and lack of a denominator mean incidence cannot be calculated

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the number exposed is unknown and most reactions are not reported.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: detecting rare reactions is a main strength.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: healthcare professionals and patients can report.

questions.explanation: Spontaneous reporting gives a numerator without a denominator, and reporting is incomplete and influenced by publicity. It therefore generates signals but cannot give rates.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman was told as a child that she was allergic to penicillin after a mild rash during an infection. She now needs antibiotics. What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Document the history accurately and consider referral for allergy assessment, since many penicillin allergy labels are not confirmed on testing
Remove the label from the record without discussion
Give penicillin at once to prove tolerance
Tell her allergies cannot be investigated

questions.correctOptionText: Document the history accurately and consider referral for allergy assessment, since many penicillin allergy labels are not confirmed on testing

distractorRationale.a: Correct: accurate history and specialist assessment are the safe route.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: removing a label without assessment risks a true allergy.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: allergy testing and challenge are available.

questions.explanation: Many labelled penicillin allergies are not true allergies, but this should be confirmed under specialist supervision. In the meantime, an alternative antibiotic is used and the reaction history is recorded in detail.

questions.stem: Describe how spontaneous reporting systems detect new drug safety signals and state two limitations.
markingGuide: Clinicians and patients report suspected reactions to a national scheme (Yellow Card, MedWatch), pooled nationally and internationally
Analysts look for clusters or disproportionality (for example PRR of 2 or more) for a drug-reaction pair
Signals are assessed with causality criteria, pharmacological plausibility and then tested by epidemiological studies
Black triangle and similar approaches encourage reporting for new drugs
Limitations: under-reporting, no denominator so no incidence, reporting bias from publicity, variable report quality
questions.explanation: Pooling many reports reveals patterns that no single clinician could see. Because the data are incomplete, signals must be verified before conclusions are drawn.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has an anaphylactic reaction shortly after his first dose of a new antibiotic. Outline how he should be counselled and what follow-up actions are needed.
markingGuide: Document the drug, timing, symptoms, severity and treatment, and record the allergy in the notes and on prescription charts
Explain which drug and related drugs to avoid in plain language
Advise carrying an alert (card or bracelet) and informing all prescribers and pharmacists
Written information; consider adrenaline auto-injector and training after anaphylaxis
Refer for specialist allergy assessment to confirm the diagnosis and define which alternatives are safe
Inform the GP and report the reaction through the national scheme
questions.explanation: The counselling aims to prevent re-exposure while keeping an accurate label. Specialist assessment and reporting complete the safety loop.

questions.stem: True or false: rechallenge with a suspected drug should be performed routinely to confirm causality.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Rechallenge can reproduce a serious or fatal reaction, so it is done only in carefully selected circumstances under specialist supervision, when benefit clearly outweighs risk. Causality is usually judged without it.
